title: अलङ्कारः — The Rhetorical Figures (Alaṅkāra) Rule Book
subtitle: Compiled from classroom source material on शब्दालङ्कार and अर्थालङ्कार (word-figures and meaning-figures), cross-referenced to standard classical alaṅkāra-śāstra terminology
source_note: Compiled from a single classroom source PDF ('08_अलङ्कारः.pdf'). IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL NOTE: unlike sandhi/samāsa/natva (which are Pāṇinian/vyākaraṇa topics governed by the Aṣṭādhyāyī), अलङ्कारशास्त्र (poetics/rhetoric) is a SEPARATE traditional discipline with its own classical authorities (Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Daṇḍin's Kāvyādarśa, Mammaṭa's Kāvyaprakāśa, Viśvanātha's Sāhityadarpaṇa, etc.), not numbered by Aṣṭādhyāyī sūtras at all. Accordingly, ashtadhyayi_ref is null throughout this file -- it would be actively misleading to invent Pāṇinian citations for this material. The 'sutra_devanagari' field is used instead for the PDF's own definitional one-liners (which function like sūtras pedagogically, even though they are not from the Aṣṭādhyāyī), and book_ref points to standard classical alaṅkāra treatises for further reading, without claiming a specific verified verse-number from any of them (I did not independently verify exact kārikā numbers against a critical edition).

how_to_read.upamana: उपमानम् -- the thing it is compared to
how_to_read.samanya_dharma: सामान्यधर्मः -- the shared quality justifying the comparison
how_to_read.upamana_vachaka: उपमानवाचकम् -- the comparison-word itself (इव, वत्, सदृश, यथा etc.)
how_to_read.process: the structural mechanism that defines this figure

shabda_alankara.english_name: Definition: alaṅkāra as ornament/embellishment of speech
shabda_alankara.rule: अलं करोति इति अलङ्कारः -- 'that which adorns/embellishes' is called अलङ्कार. In everyday usage the word means ordinary physical ornament (वस्त्रालङ्कारः, केशालङ्कारः etc.); in literary usage (साहित्ये/काव्ये) it means a deliberate, patterned arrangement of syllables/words (वर्णानां/शब्दानां विन्यासः) that enhances the beauty (सौन्दर्यम्) of a text. Alaṅkāra divides into two broad classes: शब्दालङ्कारः (figures depending on the actual sound/wording) and अर्थालङ्कारः (figures depending on the meaning, which would survive even if paraphrased into different words).

shabda_alankara.english_name: Chekānuprāsa: a single repetition of a similar consonant-cluster/sound
shabda_alankara.rule: When a similar sound (सजातीयवर्णः, meaning a full vowel+consonant unit, not just the bare consonant) occurs just ONE additional time (एकवारम् आवर्तनम्) in prose or verse, that is called छेकानुप्रासः.
shabda_alankara.book_ref: 08_अलङ्कारः.pdf; cf. Mammaṭa, Kāvyaprakāśa, chapter on śabdālaṅkāra

shabda_alankara.english_name: Vṛttyanuprāsa: repeated (more than once) repetition of a similar sound
shabda_alankara.rule: When the same sound/sound-cluster (सजातीय वर्णः or वर्णसमुदायः) recurs MANY times (अनेकवारम् आवर्तनम्), not just once, that is called वृत्त्यनुप्रासः -- distinguished from छेकानुप्रासः purely by the number of repetitions.

shabda_alankara.english_name: Yamaka: a repeated sound-sequence that carries a DIFFERENT meaning each time
shabda_alankara.rule: When a sound or sound-sequence repeats multiple times (as in वृत्त्यनुप्रासः) but, crucially, conveys a DIFFERENT meaning (भिन्नभिन्नम् अर्थम्) at each occurrence, that is called यमकम् -- distinguished from वृत्त्यनुप्रासः by this meaning-shift across repetitions, which is itself the source of the figure's cleverness.

examples.sandhi: सरस्वति प्रसादं मे स्थिरति चित्तसरस्वति। सरस्वति कुरु क्षेत्रकुरुक्षेत्रसरस्वति॥
examples.gloss: the phrase 'सरस्वति'/'कुरुक्षेत्र' recurs with shifting sense (goddess vs. one's own mental clarity vs. place-name) across the verse

artha_alankara.english_name: Upamā: simile -- explicit comparison of two distinct things sharing a quality
artha_alankara.rule: The most prominent and famous of the अर्थालङ्कारs. One thing (उपमेयम्, the subject being described) is compared to another (उपमानम्) via an explicit comparison-word (उपमानवाचकम्: इव, वत्, सदृश, यथा etc.), on the basis of a shared quality (सामान्यधर्मः). When all four components (उपमेय, उपमान, सामान्यधर्म, उपमानवाचक) are explicitly present, it is called पूर्णोपमा ("complete" simile); when the सामान्यधर्म is left unstated but understood, it is called लुप्तोपमा ("elliptical" simile).
artha_alankara.book_ref: 08_अलङ्कारः.pdf; cf. Daṇḍin, Kāvyādarśa, and Mammaṭa, Kāvyaprakāśa, on upamā and its subtypes
artha_alankara.process: उपमेयस्य उपमानेन सह सामान्यधर्मद्वारा तुलना, उपमानवाचकयुक्ता

artha_alankara.english_name: Rūpaka: metaphor -- the identity (not mere comparison) of upameya and upamāna
artha_alankara.rule: Where उपमा merely COMPARES two things (keeping them distinct), रूपक asserts their identity (अभेदः): the उपमेय IS declared to be the उपमान outright, with no comparison-word at all. The characterizing insight is इदम् एव एतद् ("this itself is that").
artha_alankara.process: उपमेयस्य उपमाने अभेद-आरोपणम्, न तु तुलना

examples.gloss: मुखं एव चन्द्रः -- the face IS declared a moon, not merely 'moon-like'
वचनानि एव कुसुमानि -- words themselves declared to be flowers

artha_alankara.english_name: Atiśayokti: hyperbole -- the upamāna stated alone, with the upameya entirely omitted
artha_alankara.rule: When only the उपमान (the thing compared TO) is mentioned, while the उपमेय (the actual subject) is left out entirely -- rather than merely having an implicit सामान्यधर्म as in लुप्तोपमा -- the resulting overstated/hyperbolic expression is called अतिशयोक्तिः.

examples.gloss: eyes described purely via the comparison-object (blue lotuses), the eyes themselves left unstated
said of a person of great valor, without naming the person

artha_alankara.english_name: Arthāntaranyāsa: corroboration -- a general statement supported by a specific one (or vice versa)
artha_alankara.rule: When a general/universal statement (सामान्यविषयः) is corroborated/justified by a specific instance (विशेषवाक्येन), or conversely a specific claim is generalized by a universal principle, the two-sentence pairing is called अर्थान्तरन्यासः.

examples.sandhi: अगस्त्यः समुद्रम् अपिबत्। किम् असाध्यं महात्मनाम्!
examples.gloss: specific feat corroborates a general maxim about great souls

examples.sandhi: जनकः अष्टावक्रं सत्कृतवान्। महात्मनः खलु गुणग्राहिणः।

artha_alankara.english_name: Śleṣa: paronomasia/pun -- one word conveying more than one meaning in the same sentence
artha_alankara.rule: When a single word, in one and the same sentence, simultaneously conveys more than one distinct meaning, that figure is called श्लेषालङ्कारः. Since a word's full meaning shifts entirely depending on which sense is intended, श्लेष is a favorite device for double-entendre verses.
artha_alankara.process: एकस्मिन् वाक्ये एकं पदम् अनेकम् अर्थं सूचयति

examples.gloss: 'कादम्बरी' = Bāṇabhaṭṭa's novel, or 'liquor' -- two readings of the same sentence
'माघे' = the poet Māgha's epic Śiśupālavadha, or the month Māgha; 'मेघे' = Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, or a rain-cloud -- the whole line reads differently under each pairing
'सर्वदः माधवः' ('the ever-giving Madhava') or 'सर्वदा उमाधवः' ('always the husband of Uma', i.e. Shiva) -- both readings valid

summary_counts.status: Covers all figures named in the source PDF: 3 śabdālaṅkāras (chekānuprāsa, vṛttyanuprāsa, yamaka) plus the general definition, and 5 arthālaṅkāras (upamā, rūpaka, atiśayokti, arthāntaranyāsa, śleṣa).
